title: How do you cut per-request overhead at the gateway: connection pooling / HTTP/2 multiplexing to reuse upstream connections instead of a new TCP+TLS handshake each time (target >99% connection reuse), hybrid rate limiting (a local token bucket synced to Redis every ~100ms instead of a Redis round trip per request), async batched logging off the request path, and request coalescing (de-duplicate identical in-flight requests)?
shortTitle: How to cut per-request overhead at the gateway
keyPoints: Connection pooling with keep-alive and HTTP/2 multiplexing reuses established connections, targeting >99% reuse.
Hybrid rate limiting keeps a local token bucket and syncs with Redis every ~100ms instead of a Redis round trip per request.
Async batched logging enqueues log events and a background worker flushes them, removing disk I/O from the request path.
Request coalescing detects identical in-flight requests and makes duplicates share one downstream call.
Each technique removes a fixed per-request cost that is multiplied by total traffic at the edge.
Coalescing applies only to idempotent, identical reads, never to distinct money-moving operations.
These optimizations must be tuned and measured: pool size, sync interval, and coalescing scope all have trade-offs.

s1_definition.oneliner: Make every request cheap by reusing upstream connections, rate limiting locally with periodic Redis sync, batching logs asynchronously, and coalescing identical in-flight requests into one downstream call.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Connection pooling** – keeps established TCP+TLS connections open and reuses them across requests, targeting over 99% reuse.
- **HTTP/2 multiplexing** – many concurrent requests share a single connection, reducing the number of connections needed.
- **Hybrid rate limiting** – a local in-memory token bucket checked instantly per request, synced with Redis every ~100ms for global consistency.
- **Async batched logging** – log events enqueued in memory and flushed by a background worker, removing I/O from the request path.
- **Request coalescing** – identical concurrent requests share one downstream call; also called single-flight or request collapsing.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine the National Bank of India dispatch desk sending documents to the central vault. If a courier sets up a new secure route for each document, that is wasteful; instead the courier keeps routes open and reuses them (connection pooling). If the clerk phones head office to check each customer's limit, that is slow; instead he keeps a local tally and syncs every few seconds (hybrid rate limiting). If he files paperwork after every customer, the line jams; instead he drops notes in a tray for batch filing (async logging). If three customers ask the same question at once, he answers once and tells all three (coalescing).

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Per-Request Overhead Reduction
  ──────────────────────────────

  Without optimization:
  Request → new connection (5ms) → rate limit Redis (0.5ms)
         → sync log (0.3ms) → downstream call → response
  Total overhead: ~5.8ms per request

  With optimization:
  Request → pooled connection (0.05ms) → local rate limit (0.01ms)
         → async log (0.001ms) → downstream call → response
  Total overhead: ~0.06ms per request

  Request Coalescing:
  100 identical requests ──▶ Coalescer ──▶ 1 downstream call
                           ◀──────────── result shared with all 100

  Hybrid Rate Limiting:
  Request → local bucket (instant) → allowed/denied
                │
                └──every 100ms──▶ Redis (sync global state)
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Cutting per-request overhead means eliminating the repeated, wasteful work the gateway does for each request, because at the edge every fixed cost is multiplied by the entire system's throughput. The four techniques are connection pooling (reuse TCP+TLS connections, targeting over 99% reuse), hybrid rate limiting (local token bucket synced with Redis every 100ms instead of a Redis call per request), async batched logging (enqueue and flush in the background, not inline), and request coalescing (identical concurrent requests share one downstream call).

At National Bank of India, applying all four cut the per-request overhead from about 5.8ms to 0.06ms. Connection pooling alone removed the biggest cost because each new TCP+TLS handshake was 5ms that multiplied by 50,000 requests per second was consuming enormous CPU and network resources. Hybrid rate limiting dropped Redis calls from 50,000 per second to 10, trading a few hundred milliseconds of global staleness for a massive reduction in latency and Redis load.

The nuances are safety and tuning. Coalescing applies only to identical, idempotent reads, never to distinct money-moving operations, because merging two different transfers would be a correctness disaster. The connection pool must be sized to avoid both contention (too small) and upstream exhaustion (too large). The rate-limit sync interval balances latency against how strict the limit must be.

Remember one sentence: remove any fixed per-request cost at the edge through connection pooling, hybrid rate limiting, async logging, and request coalescing, because at the edge every microsecond is paid by the whole system.
